Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
When Dara Ly was pulled over late one evening on his way home from a job site, he had sawdust still on his work pants and a bag of tools in the passenger seat. He remembered the red and blue lights reflecting off the windshield and the abrupt shift from an ordinary drive to a scene that felt dangerous before he could explain why. The officers shouted over one another, ordered him out of the truck, and when he hesitated for a second—trying to understand what they wanted and where to put his hands—they forced him to the ground. His cheek was pressed into the pavement, his arms wrenched behind him, and he became fixed on the sense that he could not see what was coming next. The worst part, as he later described it, was not only the pain but the helplessness of being pinned down by men who were supposed to keep people safe, while every second stretched and he did not know whether it would stop there.

In the weeks afterward, Dara did not experience the aftermath as something finished. He had come to feel that danger gathered in ordinary delays and pauses. If his wife took longer than expected to answer a text, if a foreman did not return his call, if a police cruiser idled too long at an intersection near the lumber yard, his body reacted as if something was already going wrong. He found himself scanning rooms automatically and choosing seats in diners or waiting areas where his back was against the wall and the door stayed in view. Even at home he rarely settled into the couch. He said he could know, logically, that he was in his own living room with his wife nearby and still feel unable to relax, as though some part of him was waiting to be caught off guard again.

That constant sense of threat began to shape what he did to get through the day. At work, where he moved between unfinished houses and crowded supply stores, he started arranging his breaks around where he could sit facing an entrance. If a delivery ran late or a supervisor said, “Give it a minute,” his mind jumped immediately to the idea that something bad was unfolding out of sight. In those moments he tried hard not to think about the roadside assault at all, cutting off images before they formed and pushing himself back into measuring boards, loading trim, anything concrete. When that did not work, he turned the blame inward, telling himself that if he had moved faster, spoken more clearly, or kept his hands visible in exactly the right way, none of it would have happened. Some nights he used drugs to get a break from the vigilance, because being high was the only time his body stopped bracing for a few hours. His efforts made sense to him as ways to prevent another shock or to shut down the spiraling expectation that something terrible was about to happen.

Over time, though, those habits tightened the fear rather than easing it. The more Dara cut off thoughts of the incident, the less processed it seemed, and small interruptions began carrying the same edge as that night on the pavement. Because he repeatedly blamed himself, he stayed convinced there had been a hidden mistake in his behavior that he still needed to identify, which kept him mentally reviewing the stop without reaching any relief. After using drugs, he often felt even less steady the next day, more watchful, more dependent on sitting with his back protected and his eyes on the room. What frightened him most was how quickly his mind filled in danger whenever anything took too long: a delayed paycheck, his wife lingering at the grocery store, a client not answering the door right away. He was certain these reactions were keeping him prepared, yet his world had become smaller and more rigid.

The strain has started to show in his marriage and his work. His wife sees him angle his chair toward the entrance in restaurants and go quiet when plans change unexpectedly. On jobs, coworkers have noticed that he becomes tense and irritable during delays, pacing near windows or stepping outside to calm himself. Dara finally sought help after an argument at home in which his wife told him she felt she was living beside someone always waiting for disaster. He agreed with her, though what he fears is not only staying this way. He is also afraid that if he lets himself stop watching, stop blaming himself, or stop pushing the memory away, he will be back on the ground again—unable to see, unable to stop what comes next. At the same time, he says he wants “one day where nothing feels like it’s about to happen,” and that hope is what brought him in.
